y-m-07-01.title: Can I buy a snack and a drink with 1000원?
y-m-07-01.topic: When you estimate three-digit numbers, what can you learn if the estimate equals the benchmark?
y-m-07-01.goal: Realize that when the estimate is exactly the same as the benchmark (1000원), it is hard to reach a conclusion from estimating alone. Fix your judgment and how sure you are each time new information comes in, and make an example where, even when the estimates are the same, the real values can be on both sides of the benchmark.
y-m-07-01.material: Hajun wants to buy one snack and one drink at a store. His wallet has only one 1000원 bill. All prices are natural numbers in 원. When estimating to the nearest hundred, round up if the tens digit is 5 or more and round down if it is 4 or less. For example, 460 is estimated as 500 and 440 as 400.
y-m-07-01.thinking.0: Telling apart what you can and cannot say from an estimated value
y-m-07-01.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment and how sure you are as you learn new information
y-m-07-01.thinking.2: Making different examples that meet the conditions
y-m-07-01.prereq.0: Estimating three-digit numbers to the nearest hundred (example: 487 is close to 500)
y-m-07-01.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of three-digit numbers
y-m-07-01.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what Hajun can say. You may keep your earlier thinking or fix it.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the words "about 500원" mean the real price could be greater or less than 500원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write how much greater or less than 500 each newly revealed number is, and compare those amounts with each other.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Hajun looked at the price tags from far away in front of the shelf. He read both the snack and the drink as "about 500원." (He does not know the exact numbers yet.)
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Is 1000원 enough to buy one snack and one drink?
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.after: All we know is that both prices are close to 500원. The estimate of the total equals the benchmark 1000, so from estimating alone we cannot tell whether the real total is greater or less than 1000.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 500+500=1000, so I can definitely buy them with 1000원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Just because the estimate is 1000 does not mean the real total is 1000. An estimate can be a little more or less than the real value.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The estimate is 1000, so it goes over 1000원 and I can't buy them.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The estimate 1000 is equal to the money I have, 1000원. To say it "goes over," it would have to be greater than 1000.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The estimate is exactly 1000원, so it is hard to decide from estimating alone.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This thought considered that when the estimate equals the benchmark, the real value can be greater or less than the benchmark.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I don't know the exact prices, so I can't say anything.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: An estimate is also useful information. You do know that each price is close to 500원. Work out how far you can go with that information.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.info: When he went closer and looked, the snack was 487원 and the drink was 518원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, how do you think the total of the two prices compares with 1000원?
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.after: 487 is 13 less than 500 and 518 is 18 more than 500, so the total is 5 more than 1000. Adding exactly, 487+518=1005. The judgment at first that "it is hard to decide" was still right, and now there is a reason.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The excess 18 is more than the shortfall 13, so the total is more than 1000원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This found that 518 is 18 more than 500 and 487 is 13 less than 500, and compared the amount over with the amount short. It is a good method of looking at the estimated values again with numbers.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 487 is less than 500, so the total is also less than 1000원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This left out that 518 is greater than 500. You must look at how much each price differs from 500 together.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Both are about 500, so the total is exactly 1000원 as it is.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: "About" does not mean the same. Find the difference between each price tag's number and 500.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Estimating alone doesn't tell me, so I'll add 487+518 exactly to decide.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment thinks the estimate is not enough and tries to check by calculating exactly. It is a good attitude to use estimating and calculating together.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Hajun found 2 more 10원 coins inside his wallet. Now the money he has is 1020원.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can he say when he judges with the new fact included?
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.after: 1005원 is less than 1020원, so he can buy them and 15원 is left. Even with the same prices, when the money you have changes, the conclusion changes. Deciding by the estimate 1000 alone was right this time, but its reasoning was weak.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The total is 1005원, which is more than 1000원, so he still can't buy them.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This did not put the newly found coins into the money he has. First check whether the money he has has changed.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The total 1005원 is less than the money he has, 1020원, so he can buy them.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This directly compared the changed money he has with the real total. It reflected well that new information changes the condition.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The estimate 1000 is less than 1020, so he can buy them just by looking at the estimate.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The conclusion is the same, but think back to how the estimate and the real total were different. Comparing estimates with each other is hard to trust when the difference is small.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 1005 and 1020 are similar, so we can't tell which is greater.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: 1005 and 1020 can be compared right away. Compare the sizes of the numbers to see which is greater.
y-m-07-01.s.s1.reflect: From the statement that the estimate at first was 1000, what could you tell and what could you not tell? After seeing the exact numbers on the price tags, and after finding more coins, how did your thinking or how sure you were change? If you kept your first thinking as it was, say why too.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two pairs of prices where the total of the estimates is 1000원 but the real total is not 1000원. One pair must have a total greater than 1000원, and the other pair must have a total less than 1000원. The snack a원 and the drink b원 are each natural numbers from 100원 to 999원.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.0: Start by making the pair with a total greater than 1000. Let one price be a little above 500 and the other price a little below 500.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.hint.1: Once you have made one pair, swap the amount above and the amount below to make a pair whose total is less than 1000.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.ok.c1: Both prices are natural numbers from 100원 to 999원.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Both prices must be natural numbers from 100 to 999.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.ok.c2: Estimating each to the nearest hundred and adding gives 1000.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Estimating each price to the nearest hundred and adding does not give 1000. Check the rule that you round up if the tens digit is 5 or more.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.fail.c3: If the real total is exactly 1000원, it is the same as the estimate, so it is not an example.
y-m-07-01.s.s2.explain: 487+518=1005 is greater than 1000, and 480+510=990 is less than 1000. Even when the estimates are the same, 1000, the real totals can be on both sides of the benchmark. So when the estimate equals the benchmark, do not decide from estimating alone; look more closely.

y-m-07-02.title: 6 bags with 47 marbles each, three ways to calculate
y-m-07-02.topic: Several ways to calculate (two-digit number)×(one-digit number) by splitting a number
y-m-07-02.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in ways of calculating by splitting a number, and check with your own example that making the split in different ways gives the same total, then say why.
y-m-07-02.thinking.0: Comparing three solutions and finding the error
y-m-07-02.thinking.1: Making several ways to split within the conditions
y-m-07-02.thinking.2: Explaining why the results are the same even when the methods differ
y-m-07-02.prereq.1: Multiplying tens by a one-digit number (example: 40×6)
y-m-07-02.prereq.2: Having done (two-digit number)×(one-digit number) in vertical form
y-m-07-02.s.s1.prompt: These are the three friends' calculations. Choose one line where the calculation is wrong.
y-m-07-02.s.s1.hint.0: First compare line by line how the three friends rewrote 47.
y-m-07-02.s.s1.line.1: Jian: 240+42=282. There are 282 marbles in all.
y-m-07-02.s.s1.line.3: Doha: 300+18=318. There are 318 marbles in all.
y-m-07-02.s.s1.line.5: Seoa: 270+12=282. There are 282 marbles in all.
y-m-07-02.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. Doha saw 47 as "3 less than 50," so from 50×6=300 he must take away 3×6=18, which gives 300−18=282. Adding makes it as if he calculated with 53 instead of 47. Jian's and Seoa's calculations both give the same 282.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to calculate 47×6 by splitting 47 into two numbers a and b. Make 3 different splits that are easy to calculate. Conditions: a and b are natural numbers and a+b=47. And one of the two must be a number that appears in the 5s multiplication table (a multiple of 5). Splitting into 40 and 7 and splitting into 7 and 40 count as the same split.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.0: First check whether a and b add up to 47.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a number from the 5s multiplication table, subtract it from 47, and find the other number.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.ok.c2: a and b add up to 47.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of a and b is not 47.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.ok.c3: One of the two is a number in the 5s multiplication table.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.fail.c3: At least one of a and b must be a multiple of 5 (5, 10, 15, ...).
y-m-07-02.s.s2.explain: For example, 40+7, 45+2, 35+12, and 30+17 all add up to 47 and have one number that is a multiple of 5. However you split it, adding (split number)×6 gives 47×6=282.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.prompt: When you calculated each split you made, how many marbles did you get? In one or two sentences, write why the result is the same even when the way of splitting differs.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the result you got for each split you made in one place and compare them.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about whether the total number of marbles could change depending on the order in which you count 6 bags of 47.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: There are ... marbles. Even if I change how I split, ... because ...
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the result was the same 282 for all the splits you made?
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words that "splitting 47, calculating, and putting it back together" does not change the total number of marbles?
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you connect the condition that the split numbers add up to 47 with the reason the result is the same?
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.model.0: There are 282 marbles in all. However you split 47, you are putting back together the count of 6 bags of 47 that you counted in parts, so the total stays the same.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.model.1: I got 282 marbles. Whether you add 40×6 and 7×6 or add 45×6 and 2×6, the total number of marbles is the same, so the result is the same.
y-m-07-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: I explained by giving two examples of my own with different ways of splitting.

y-m-07-03.title: The same calculation, but the answer changes with each story
y-m-07-03.topic: Cases where the quotient and the remainder in a division with a remainder are used differently in different stories
y-m-07-03.goal: Interpret the result (quotient, remainder) of a division with a remainder to fit the question in the story, and make stories yourself where the same calculation gives different answers.
y-m-07-03.material: On the autumn field trip, 50 students ride boats. All the boats are the same size and each can carry up to 8 people. No student can be left out. When you calculate 50÷8 (fifty divided by eight), the quotient is 6 and the remainder is 2. You can check this with 8×6+2=50.
y-m-07-03.thinking.0: Interpreting a mathematical result to fit the question in a situation
y-m-07-03.thinking.1: Making a situation that meets the conditions
y-m-07-03.thinking.2: Making stories where the same calculation gives different answers
y-m-07-03.prereq.0: The meaning of quotient and remainder in division (the remainder is less than the divisor)
y-m-07-03.prereq.1: The relationship between multiplication and division (8×6+2=50)
y-m-07-03.prereq.2: Simple division with numbers up to 100
y-m-07-03.s.s1.prompt: For all 50 students to ride, how many boats must there be at least?
y-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw 8 people to a boat in a picture or a table and count how many boats are full.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.hint.1: Find how many people are left after the full boats, and think about where those people should ride.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.r.a: This read the quotient 6 directly as the number of boats. Check whether any students could not ride in the 6 full boats.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.r.b: This read the capacity of 8 people as the number of boats. 8 is the number of people one boat can carry.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.r.c: This read the remainder 2 as the number of boats. 2 is the number of people left over.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.r.d: This put into the calculation result the condition that the leftover students need a place to ride.
y-m-07-03.s.s1.explain: 6 boats carry 48 people and 2 are left over. The 2 left must ride too, so one more boat is needed, which makes 7 boats. In this story, the answer is not the quotient 6 but the number one greater than the quotient.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.prompt: If the number of students changes, the number of boats needed changes too. Make 3 situations where exactly 10 boats are needed and the last boat is not filled to capacity. The number of students is n and the capacity of one boat is c. The capacity is a natural number from 2 to 9, and all students must ride.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a capacity, then change the number of students near the value of adding the capacity 9 times, and count the boats needed.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.hint.1: Once you have chosen the number of students, find the quotient and remainder of the division and check whether any students are left over.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of students and the capacity are natural numbers.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of students and the capacity must be natural numbers.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The capacity is from 2 to 9 people.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The capacity must be from 2 to 9 people.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The last boat is not filled to capacity.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c3: If the number of students is divisible by the capacity, all the boats are full. The last boat must be less than full.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.ok.c4: For all students to ride, exactly 10 boats are needed.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The boats needed are not 10. Divide the number of students by the capacity and check the full boats and the leftover students.
y-m-07-03.s.s2.explain: For example, with 75 students and capacity 8, the quotient of 75÷8 is 9 and the remainder is 3. The 3 students left over after 9 full boats need one more boat, so it is 10. Even with the same capacity, depending on the number of students the quotient can stay the same while only the remainder changes.
y-m-07-03.s.s3.prompt: Using the same calculation 50÷8=6…2 (quotient 6, remainder 2), make one story where the answer is 6 and one story where the answer is 2. Be sure to use 50 and 8 in the stories.
y-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think of other stories about dividing things into containers or dividing up purchases, like buying things with 50원.
y-m-07-03.s.s3.hint.1: Decide whether the last question of your story asks "how many times/how many can you fit" or "how many are left over."
y-m-07-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Story where the answer is 6: ... / Story where the answer is 2: ...
y-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the story where the answer is 6, does the question ask for the "quotient"?
y-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the story where the answer is 2, does the question ask for "what is left over"?
y-m-07-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do both stories use 50 and 8 as they are, and is the calculation the same as 50÷8?
y-m-07-03.s.s3.model.0: Answer 6: If you buy 8원 candies with 50원, you can buy 6. Answer 2: If you tie 50 books in bundles of 8, 2 books are left over.
y-m-07-03.s.s3.model.1: Answer 6: If you cut a 50cm string into 8cm pieces, you get 6 pieces. Answer 2: If you share 50 candies equally among 8 people, each person gets 6 and 2 are left over.
y-m-07-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: I made it clear that the question of the second story is the "number left over."

y-m-07-04.title: After 285 of 603 books were borrowed, a strange calculation result
y-m-07-04.topic: Cases where calculating one digit at a time in vertical subtraction of three-digit numbers is right and cases where it is wrong
y-m-07-04.goal: Find the wrong line in a vertical-subtraction solution, choose ways to check that the result is strange, and find, with examples, the conditions under which that wrong way happens to be right.
y-m-07-04.material: The library had 603 books, and 285 of them were borrowed. Eunu calculated in vertical form how many books were left and said "482 books." 603−285 is read "six hundred three minus two hundred eighty-five." Eunu's steps for the calculation are given as lines in the next part.
y-m-07-04.thinking.0: Finding the location of the error in the solution steps
y-m-07-04.thinking.1: Comparing the strength of different checking methods
y-m-07-04.thinking.2: Finding the conditions under which a wrong method is right
y-m-07-04.prereq.0: Having done vertical subtraction of three-digit numbers (knowing what borrowing is)
y-m-07-04.prereq.2: Having checked a calculation result with another calculation
y-m-07-04.s.s1.prompt: These are Eunu's calculation steps. Choose one line that is wrong.
y-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.0: In the vertical form, follow line by line what Eunu did, starting from the ones place.
y-m-07-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look at what Eunu did when the top number was less than the bottom number, and think about whether it is the same as "subtracting 285 from 603."
y-m-07-04.s.s1.line.0: Write 603−285 vertically and calculate starting from the ones place.
y-m-07-04.s.s1.line.1: Ones place: Can't subtract 5 from 3, so write 5−3=2.
y-m-07-04.s.s1.line.2: Tens place: Can't subtract 8 from 0, so write 8−0=8.
y-m-07-04.s.s1.explain: Line 2 and line 3 are wrong. When the top number is less than the bottom number and you can't subtract, Eunu swapped the two numbers and subtracted. In that case, you must take 10 from the place just above and subtract (borrowing). Doing it this way, 603−285=318.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to find out that Eunu's answer 482 is strange.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each checking method, think about "does the mistake show up even if you make the same mistake as Eunu?"
y-m-07-04.s.s2.o.a: Calculate again from the beginning in the same way as Eunu.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.r.a: If you use the same method, the same mistake repeats and the same value comes out. You need a different method.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.o.b: Add 482 and 285 and check whether you get 603.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.r.b: This thought of checking the result of a subtraction by going back with addition. It is a different path from Eunu's method, so it can catch the mistake.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.o.c: See whether the 482 books left are fewer than the 603 books at the start.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.r.c: 482 is less than 603. A wrong answer also passes this condition, so this alone cannot reveal the mistake.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.o.d: Estimate 603 and 285 and see roughly how many books will be left.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.r.d: This is a method of estimating and comparing with 482. You can find an answer that is far off without detailed calculation.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.explain: 482+285=767, which is not 603, so it is wrong. Also, 603 is about 600 and 285 is about 300, so about 300 books are left, but 482 is much more than that. Calculating again the same way or only looking at whether 482 is less than 603 cannot reveal the mistake.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.acc.0: Checking by adding is exact. See whether you can also check by estimating.
y-m-07-04.s.s2.acc.1: You found by estimating that it is far off. See whether there is also a way to check exactly by adding.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.prompt: There are also subtractions where Eunu's method (subtracting the smaller number from the larger number in each place and writing it) happens to be right. Make 2 different subtractions where the value calculated by Eunu's method equals the correct result. Subtract a three-digit number b from a three-digit number a (a must be greater than b). Eunu's method is to write the difference of the two digits (the larger digit minus the smaller digit) in each of the hundreds, tens, and ones places.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.0: Find both the value from Eunu's method and the value from the usual method, and compare whether they are the same.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write in a table which of the top and bottom digits is greater in each place, and find where the wrong examples and the right examples split.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.ok.c1: a is a three-digit number greater than b.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b are three-digit natural numbers and a must be greater than b.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.ok.c2: The value from Eunu's method equals the correct result.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.fail.c2: The value from Eunu's method differs from the correct result. Compare the digits in each place.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.explain: For example, 587−243 gives 7−3=4, 8−4=4, 5−2=3, so by Eunu's method it is 344, and the correct result is also 344. In cases like this, where every place has a top digit that is greater than or equal to the bottom digit, no borrowing is needed, so Eunu's method is right too.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.prompt: Looking at the examples where Eunu's method came out right, what kind of subtraction are they? Compare the digits in each place and write one or two sentences.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.0: Put the examples you made side by side and write in a table which is greater, the top digit or the bottom digit, in each place.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.hint.1: In 603−285, where Eunu's method was wrong, find and compare in which place the top digit is less than the bottom digit.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: In each place, the top digit is ...
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: In the examples you made, did you check that there was no place where the top digit was less than the bottom digit?
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write what "no borrowing is needed" means in your own words?
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Can you connect which place broke this condition in the wrong example (603−285)?
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.0: It was a subtraction with no borrowing. In 587−243, like 7−3, 8−4, and 5−2, the top digit is greater than the bottom digit in every place, so doing it like Eunu is right too.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.model.1: It was right when the top digit was greater than or equal to the bottom digit in each place. It was a subtraction where you did not have to borrow.
y-m-07-04.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: I wrote the condition that no borrowing is needed in my own words.

y-m-07-05.title: 1/2 and 1/4 of a ribbon: who used more?
y-m-07-05.topic: Fractions can be compared in size only when the whole is the same (fractions of different wholes)
y-m-07-05.goal: Realize that fractions of different wholes cannot be compared by the size of the fractions alone, sort out what information makes comparing possible, and find with numbers cases where the lengths the two people used are the same.
y-m-07-05.material: Jian used 1/2 of a red ribbon, and Doyun used 1/4 of a blue ribbon. We do not know whether the two ribbons were the same length at first. Each ribbon was a single uncut strip, and 1/2 and 1/4 mean the whole of each person's own ribbon divided into equal parts. 1/2 is read "one half" and 1/4 is read "one quarter."
y-m-07-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-07-05.thinking.1: Finding the conditions needed for comparing
y-m-07-05.thinking.2: Testing the conditions with specific numbers
y-m-07-05.prereq.0: That a fraction shows how many of the equal parts of a whole there are
y-m-07-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose what you can say about who used the longer ribbon, using only what you know now.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.hint.0: Decide the lengths of the red ribbon and the blue ribbon however you like (example: 20cm, 40cm) and write the lengths the two people used in cm.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.hint.1: Change the lengths of the ribbons and check whether who uses more changes.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.o.a: We do not know the starting lengths of the two ribbons, so we cannot decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.r.a: This pointed out that a fraction is about "its own whole." Think about what more information would let you decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.o.b: It is Jian, because 1/2 is greater than 1/4.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.r.b: 1/2 is greater than 1/4 only when compared in the same whole. First look at whether the wholes of the two ribbons are the same.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.o.c: It is Doyun, because the denominator 4 is greater than 2.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.r.c: A greater denominator does not make the length used longer. If the wholes are different, how many cm it is changes.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.o.d: It is probably Jian. It is rare for the wholes to be different.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.r.d: There is no basis for stating that it is "rare." Test with numbers what happens if the ribbons have different wholes.
y-m-07-05.s.s1.explain: 1/2 is greater than 1/4 when compared in the same whole (ribbons of the same length). For example, if the red ribbon is 20cm, 1/2 is 10cm, but if the blue ribbon is 80cm, 1/4 is 20cm, which is longer, and if the blue ribbon is 8cm, 1/4 is 2cm, which is shorter. You need to know the lengths of the two ribbons to decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information such that knowing just that one more thing lets you decide who used more. (Think about each choice separately.)
y-m-07-05.s.s2.hint.0: Assume the information is true, set the red ribbon at 20cm, make examples of the blue ribbon's length one at a time, and find the lengths the two people used.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.hint.1: For each piece of information, make two or more different examples of the blue ribbon's length and check whether the conclusion is always the same.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.o.a: The blue ribbon is longer than the red ribbon.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.r.a: "Longer" alone does not tell you how much longer. Test the case where the blue ribbon is around 2 times the red ribbon.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.o.b: The two ribbons are the same length at first.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.r.b: You know that if the wholes are the same, you can compare the sizes of fractions right away.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.o.c: Both people used half or less of their own ribbons.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.r.c: 1/2 and 1/4 are already half or less. You have not learned anything new.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.o.d: The blue ribbon is shorter than the red ribbon.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.r.d: If the blue ribbon is shorter, its 1/4 is even shorter, and you can compare it with 1/2 of the red ribbon. This used the relationship between the sizes of the wholes.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.o.e: The blue ribbon is 4 times the length of the red ribbon.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.r.e: This is information that gives the relationship between the sizes of the wholes as an exact multiple. You can change 1/4 to be in terms of the red ribbon.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.explain: Call the red ribbon R and the blue ribbon B. Then Jian used half of R and Doyun used 1/4 of B. If the two ribbons are the same, Jian uses more. If the blue ribbon is shorter, Jian still uses more. If the blue ribbon is 4 times as long, Doyun uses as much as R, so Doyun uses more. Knowing only that the blue ribbon is longer, you can't tell if it is more than 2 times as long, so you can't decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.acc.0: You chose a correct piece of information. Test whether the information that it is 4 times as long can also let you decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.acc.1: You chose a correct piece of information. Test whether the information "it is shorter" can also let you decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s2.acc.2: You chose a correct piece of information. Test whether the information "the starting lengths are the same" can also let you decide.
y-m-07-05.s.s3.prompt: Say the red ribbon is 20cm. How many cm would the blue ribbon be for the two people to have used the same length? Also write who used more if the blue ribbon is longer than that. (Ribbons can be divided into equal parts.)
y-m-07-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many cm half of the red ribbon is.
y-m-07-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how many cm the whole blue ribbon must be for one of its 4 equal parts to be that length.
y-m-07-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the blue ribbon is ...cm, they are the same. This is because ...
y-m-07-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you first find how many cm 1/2 of the 20cm red ribbon is, and compare it with one part of the blue ribbon divided into 4 parts?
y-m-07-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write separately for when the blue ribbon is longer than 40cm and when it is shorter?
y-m-07-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do you know that the conclusion you wrote is a story under the condition "when the red ribbon is 20cm"?
y-m-07-05.s.s3.model.0: They are the same when the blue ribbon is 40cm. 1/2 of 20cm is 10cm and 1/4 of 40cm is also 10cm. If it is longer than 40cm, 1/4 is longer than 10cm, so Doyun uses more.
y-m-07-05.s.s3.model.1: It is 40cm. Half of the red ribbon is 10cm, and one part of the blue ribbon divided into 4 equal parts must be 10cm. If the blue ribbon is longer, one part is longer than 10cm, so Doyun uses more.
y-m-07-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: I explained by dividing into parts.

y-m-07-06.title: 3 number cards: where does the product get bigger?
y-m-07-06.topic: Finding cases with a big product when making (two-digit number)×(one-digit number) expressions with number cards
y-m-07-06.goal: Test the idea "if you make the largest two-digit number, the product is also the largest" by making expressions yourself, find several expressions with a big product, and write why.
y-m-07-06.material: There is one each of the number cards 3, 5, and 7. Use every card exactly once to make a (two-digit number)×(one-digit number) expression. For example, place 3 and 5 side by side to make 35 and multiply by 7, giving 35×7 (thirty-five times seven). Do not flip the cards. Harin said, "If I make the largest two-digit number, 75, and multiply by 3, the product will be the biggest!"
y-m-07-06.thinking.1: Making several expressions that meet the conditions
y-m-07-06.thinking.2: Explaining why the product gets bigger
y-m-07-06.prereq.1: How to make a two-digit number with number cards (tens place, ones place)
y-m-07-06.prereq.2: Comparing the sizes of two numbers
y-m-07-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the judgment you can make now about what Harin said.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.hint.1: First count how many expressions in all can be made with the 3 cards.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.o.a: It is right. When the two-digit number is the largest, the product is also the largest.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.r.a: The one-digit number you multiply by also changes depending on the cards. You must not look only at the two-digit number.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.o.b: We do not know yet. We need to compare it with the products of other card arrangements.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.r.b: This saw that you must test whether the claim is right by comparing with other expressions. It is a good judgment of trying to gather evidence.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.o.c: It does not seem right. The multiplier 3 is small, so it may be a loss.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.r.c: This pointed out that the multiplier gets smaller. But since it is a guess, you need to check by comparing with other expressions.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.o.d: The product is similar however you place them, so there is no need to compare.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.r.d: Before deciding the products are similar, calculate a few expressions yourself. They could be very different.
y-m-07-06.s.s1.acc.0: This is a reasonable guess. But since it is a guess, you must find the products yourself to check.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different expressions with a product greater than 240. The tens card is t, the ones card is u, and the multiplying card is m. You must use the cards 3, 5, and 7 once each.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.0: Place one card each in the tens place, the ones place, and the multiplier place and calculate the product.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.hint.1: Taking the product of 75×3 as the standard, compare how the product changes when you change the place where you put 7.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All three places are one of 3, 5, or 7.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c1: You can only use the cards 3, 5, and 7.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.ok.c2: You used each card exactly once.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c2: You must not use the same card twice. You must use 3, 5, and 7 once each.
y-m-07-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The product is not greater than 240. Try changing the places of the cards.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.prompt: Of the 6 expressions that can be made with the cards 3, 5, and 7, which expression has the greatest product? And write why Harin's method (75×3) did not give the greatest product.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the products of all 6 expressions, write them in a table, and circle the greatest.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare which card is the multiplier in the expression with the greatest product and in Harin's expression.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The expression with the greatest product is ... Harin's method ... because ...
y-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you decide on the greatest product after calculating all 6?
y-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare where 7 is placed in Harin's expression and in the expression with the greatest product?
y-m-07-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write in your own words why the method "make only the two-digit number big" is not enough?
y-m-07-06.s.s3.model.0: The greatest product is 53×7=371. If you make 75 like Harin, the multiplier is 3, so 75×3=225 is smaller. Using the big number 7 as the multiplier was bigger.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.model.1: Using 7 as the multiplier and making 53 with the rest, 53×7=371, is the biggest. 75×3=225, so Harin's method was not right.
y-m-07-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: You can also compare it with 73×5=365.
